strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: predicting answer failures before generation. A lightweight probe over frozen question representations offers a practical way to reduce prediction costs without modifying the underlying LLM.

Table 1 provides encouraging evidence across three models and three datasets. The middle-layer, last-token probe achieves 86.5–88.7 AUC on PopQA and 85.0–85.6 on Entity Questions, generally matching or exceeding full fine-tuning. Table 2 reports substantial efficiency benefits and explicitly accounts for representation extraction.

The reported cross-model adaptation gains are substantial: for example, LLaMA2-to-LLaMA3 transfer on PopQA improves from 44.3 to 84.2 AUC. The aligned-batch ablation and additional Gemma experiment provide useful evidence beyond the main comparisons.

The manuscript includes informative ablations of representation pooling, layers, training size, and adaptation kernels. The size-matched dataset comparison and discussion of temporal and reasoning failures help characterize limitations. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b04/review-experiment-_vlx9v1d/call-b70b3fd8eb684077acc8226ddd48df76/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central claim of negligible concept shift is not established by Section 5.1. A mixture-trained network can recognize model-specific regions of representation space and implement different predictors while matching each individual probe. Comparable AUC and small individual-versus-mixture prediction gaps therefore do not demonstrate shared conditional distributions. Likewise, Equation 7 asserts a strict improvement in distribution-distance estimation without assumptions or proof; aligned sampling need not improve every batch.

Important controls are missing for interpreting the predictive signal and transfer gains. Question-text or generic-embedding classifiers would help distinguish model-specific knowledge signals from question difficulty and topic familiarity. Because training questions are paired across models, a particularly relevant baseline is training a target-representation probe directly with source-model correctness labels. Without this comparison or evaluation on questions where models disagree in correctness, adaptation may primarily exploit correlated answerability.

Label quality is only partially validated. Exact substring matching can reject correct alternative expressions and accept answers that mention the gold answer in a negation or contradiction. The audit covers 180 instances labeled factual, leaving the claim that all non-factual instances are correctly labeled unsupported. Audit both classes. Including abstentions follows the stated definition, but the resulting evidence concerns failure to supply the requested answer rather than factuality of every generated claim.

The unsupervised adaptation protocol needs clearer reproducibility details. The manuscript does not specify a target-label-free rule for selecting adaptation checkpoints and kernels, or clearly document synchronized question-level splits across models. These omissions do not establish leakage, but prevent verifying its exclusion. Exact answer-generation prompts/chat templates, split identifiers or seeds, and implementation artifacts are also missing, despite useful architectural and optimization details in Appendix D.

The evidence for robustness and practical reliability remains limited. Results lack repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, making small layer differences difficult to interpret. Performance falls to 68.9–71.4 AUC on the filtered, 1,244-question Natural Questions subset; random splits on template-based datasets do not establish generalization to unseen topics. AUC and the informal volunteer ratings also do not establish probability calibration or effective failure prevention. The promising empirical results make Findings plausible, but the unresolved central interpretation and adaptation-protocol concerns prevent a clear positive recommendation.
